title: Hydrogen: Contention-Aware Hybrid Memory for Heterogeneous CPU-GPU Architectures
problem: CPUs and GPUs in heterogeneous systems exhibit distinct preferences for memory capacity versus bandwidth, causing contention and suboptimal resource utilization. Existing designs couple capacity and bandwidth allocation, preventing performance-optimized distribution.
motivation: Efficient hybrid memory allocation across heterogeneous processors can improve system efficiency and maintain performance isolation in CPU-GPU systems.
method: Hydrogen separates memory capacity from bandwidth for CPUs and GPUs, letting each processor get a flexible split rather than a fixed one. To prevent GPU data transfers from overwhelming the system, it uses a token-based throttle where transfers only happen when a processor has a token to spend. The system automatically finds the best configuration by testing different settings in repeating time cycles called epochs, switching between them with minimal overhead.
key_novelty: The key insight is decoupling memory capacity from bandwidth, then continuously optimizing how much of each the CPU and GPU get by testing different settings in repeating cycles (epochs).
contributions: Decoupled capacity and bandwidth allocation with flexible partitioning ratios between CPUs and GPUs
Token-based throttling mechanism for controlling GPU data migration
Epoch-based online search for exploring multi-dimensional design space optimization
Lightweight reconfiguration approach reducing data movement costs
limitations: Specific baseline systems, evaluation workloads, and scalability to diverse architectures not discussed in abstract.
